summary: POC scoping call focused on data handling constraints for a merchant payments POC: PII redaction, prompt storage policy, retention windows, and a three-week benchmark timeline. Agreed success criteria: p95 latency under 250ms for short routing flows, zero-card PANs in logs, configurable retention to 30/7/0 days, and reproducible benchmark runs. transcript:
[00:00] Owen Mitchell: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — we'll keep to about 40 minutes, lots to get through on the POC scope. Uh, quick roll call?
[00:08] Carlos Vega: Carlos here, hi.
[00:10] Anika Basu: Anika, security.
[00:12] Jamal Reed: Jamal, product.
[00:14] Priya Nair: Priya from Redwood, SE.
[00:16] Owen Mitchell: Great. Objective today: align on success criteria, the dataset for benchmarks, and the timeline for the pilot. I'll hand off to Priya for a short sketch of the bench approach.
[00:28] Priya Nair: Cool. So the way we normally run these merchant-oriented benchs is, eh, three phases: ingest + config, redaction & policy validation, and full perf runs. We'll want a tokenized sample of your traffic, ideally a week of representative requests — not full PANs, please — so we can replay at scale. Typical ask is 50k to 200k request samples depending on how varied the prompts are.
[00:53] Jamal Reed: When you say "replay at scale" what's the concurrency we should expect? Our production see peaks of about 350 rps for payment routing callouts.
[01:02] Priya Nair: Good question. For the POC we usually test at three operating points: baseline (10 rps), expected (100-150 rps), and stress (350-500 rps) to measure p50/p95/p99. We'll also test short seqs (20-64 tokens) and longer contextual flows (200+ tokens) because those change KV cache and batching behavior.
[01:20] Anika Basu: On the PII front — our compliance constraint is no card PANs or CVC in logs ever. We also prefer not to send raw card numbers to hosted vendors; we'd like to see both a hosted and private option.
[01:33] Owen Mitchell: Understood. We can do two parallel runs: hosted (Redwood API) with prompt sanitization + redaction hooks, and a private deployment in your VPC where you can enable customer-side KMS for envelope encryption. Priya, can you summarize the redaction options?
[01:48] Priya Nair: Yeah. There's an inline redaction pre-processor we run client-side — strtok — uh, sorry, that was a mis-speech — the idea is a prehook that replaces patterns (PAN regexes) with stable tokens. We also support server-side masking in logs where the console will show only hashed tokens. For full private, you keep the plaintext inside your VPC and we never persist prompts on our control plane if you choose zero-persist mode.
[02:10] Anika Basu: Zero-persist mode — can you confirm that means no prompt storage on Redwood side?
[02:15] Priya Nair: Correct. Zero-persist means no prompts stored beyond in-memory processing and ephemeral logs necessary for the request; customers can opt out of any logging that contains prompt text. We'll also provide an audit trail of request IDs and SHA256 digests if you need to correlate without the content.
[02:29] Carlos Vega: How about retention windows — we have differences across teams. For some telemetry we need 30 days, for sensitive prompts we want 7 days default and auto-delete. Is that supported?
[02:37] Priya Nair: Yep. Retention is configurable per-route. Typical presets are 30d (analytics), 7d (sensitive prompts), and 0d (no retention). We can also add a retention-tagging policy during ingest so you don't have to change requests, just tag the session.
[02:49] Jamal Reed: And deletion on demand? If a user requests erasure, how fast is the remove?
[02:54] Priya Nair: We support API-driven deletion; from initiation to background job it’s typically under 24 hours for most runs. For Private deployment with your own S3, deletion is immediate once you delete the object.
[03:05] Anika Basu: Encryption — KMS? We require HSM backed keys for production.
[03:09] Owen Mitchell: We integrate with customer KMS (AWS KMS, GCP CMEK) and can support an HSM-backed key via external KMS. For Dedicated we can also offer a bring-your-own-key flow and SAML-based RBAC mapping. We'll include our key flow docs in the security pack.
[03:22] Priya Nair: One note: in hosted mode, while keys are customer-managed for certain flows, the compute is shared; for highest isolation you should look at Private (VPC/on-prem) or Dedicated pools.
[03:30] Carlos Vega: Okay. Bench numbers — you mentioned target latencies earlier. For payment routing we need sub-300ms p95 for the short calls. Is that realistic?
[03:37] Priya Nair: For short seq requests (<=64 tokens) on a quantized 8-bit model on a GPU instance, we've seen p95 around 120–220ms depending on batching. With continuous batching disabled (low latency mode) you can hit lower tail latency at cost of throughput. For p95 < 250ms at ~150 rps that's in-scope; for 350 rps we may need dedicated pools or model sharding.
[03:57] Jamal Reed: Sharding? Like splitting the KV cache?
[03:59] Priya Nair: More like model-pinning and sharding across GPUs. The runtime can do model parallel or instance scaling. We'll propose a config in the benchmark spreadsheet that maps concurrent clients to reserved GPU capacity.
[04:10] Anika Basu: How deterministic are the perf runs? We need reproducible runs for SRE signoff.
[04:15] Priya Nair: We'll provide a runbook and a Jupyter that replays the same seeds. We log seed, model version, quantization profile, runtime args, and metrics. Expect a +/- 10% variance in p95 across runs on shared hardware; on Dedicated/Private it's much tighter.
[04:30] Carlos Vega: Can we avoid sending real user identifiers even hashed? Our legal team is picky.
[04:35] Owen Mitchell: Totally — you can tokenized identifiers with a one-way mapping that only you keep. Our recommended pattern: replace PII with stable token IDs before sending, keep a mapping offline in your KMS-protected vault. That way Redwood only sees the token. We'll show the sample pre-processor code.
[04:48] Jamal Reed: For the POC success criteria, let's propose: 1) functional parity for routing logic on sample set, 2) p95 < 250ms at 150 rps for short flows, 3) zero PANs in any persisted logs, 4) bench run reproducible and documented.
[05:05] Owen Mitchell: Sounds good. Priya, any additions?
[05:07] Priya Nair: Add cost per 1M tokens estimate and a fallback policy test — e.g., when load spikes beyond dedicated pool, we validate fallback to a smaller model with graceful degradation. Also include availability targets for the POC — we usually expect 99.5% during bench windows.
[05:20] Anika Basu: On the security docs, please send SOC 2 Type II report and pen test summary. Also SSO/SAML setup details for RBAC. Jamal, are you ok with a 3-week pilot?
[05:30] Jamal Reed: Yes, 3 weeks sounds right. Week 1: dataset and config + redaction validation. Week 2: perf runs at baseline + expected. Week 3: full stress + report and handoff.
[05:40] Owen Mitchell: We'll aim for that. Tentative timeline: Kickoff week of 2025-09-15, finish by 2025-10-06. Any blockers to that schedule?
[05:49] Carlos Vega: Only getting the sanitized dataset out of our data lake — security needs to sign off. I'll push to get it by 9/10.
[05:56] Priya Nair: I'll prepare the bench spreadsheet and include three preset run configs: light, typical, heavy. Link to the sheet will be: https://drive.google.com/drive/fake-redwood-bench/merc-poc (placeholder).
[06:08] Owen Mitchell: Security artifacts link: https://redwood.example.com/enterprises/security-pack (we'll attach SOC2, KMS flow diagrams, pen test).
[06:16] Anika Basu: One other question — prompt storage for debug. We sometimes want a very short window (24h) so product can debug issues then purge. Can you do 24h retention?
[06:24] Priya Nair: Yes, retention can be set to 1d for debug routes. We'll recommend using route tags so debug traffic is automatically treated differently.
[06:32] Jamal Reed: For the dataset, what's the minimum size to get meaningful throughput numbers?
[06:36] Priya Nair: Minimum 10k requests with representative distribution. If you can't provide that, we can synthetically expand a smaller dataset but it's less ideal.
[06:44] Carlos Vega: Regarding legal and procurement — do you require an NDA before we share sanitized data?
[06:48] Owen Mitchell: We generally exchange a mutual NDA for PII-sanitized sets; for tokenized samples often we can proceed under a mutual non-prod data agreement. I'll send the legal contact and a one-pager.
[06:57] Anika Basu: Can we get a checklist of what you need included in the sample export? Fields, redaction notes, expected pivots?
[07:02] Priya Nair: Yes — I'll include a sample CSV schema and the pre-processing script.
[07:07] Owen Mitchell: Quick recap of next steps: Owen sends security pack & legal contact by tomorrow; Priya shares bench spreadsheet & runbook by 9/12; Carlos to upload tokenized sample by 9/10; schedule kickoff week of 9/15.
[07:21] Jamal Reed: That captures it. Anything else?
[07:24] Carlos Vega: One small ask — include an example of the masking that would appear in the Console so security can see what logs look like.
[07:30] Priya Nair: Will do, sample screenshots and redaction examples included in the pack.
[07:34] Owen Mitchell: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with the links.
[07:37] Anika Basu: Thanks.
[07:38] All: Bye.
[07:40] End of call.

Notes: Transcription contains occasional mis-heard terms ("strtok" for tokenizer, "sock-two" reference to SOC2), filler words, and timestamp alignment every ~15-20s. Shared artifacts: benchmark sheet (drive link), security pack (redwood link).
